newsitem.title: JORDAN: Aramex courier invests in Asia after U.S. listing.
newsitem.headline: Aramex courier invests in Asia after U.S. listing.

text.p: Middle East courier firm Aramex International said on Wednesday it would use $7 million revenue from its listing on the New York stock exchange to expand in the Indian subcontinent and former Soviet republics.
Shares in Jordan-based Aramex, which says it is the first private Arab company to go public in the United States, started trading in New York last week.
Aramex president Fadi Ghandour said the courier and freight forwarding firm aimed at setting up joint ventures in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, and build on its presence in Uzbekistan.
"They are very exciting markets -- growing nicely for freight forwarding and express," Ghandour told Reuters. "We are now finalising negotiations in the Indian subcontinent...for joint ventures."
Profits for the first nine months of 1996 stood at $1.45 million, nearly double the figure for the whole of 1995.
Ghandour said Aramex, which has stations in the Middle East, Asia, the United States, Canada, and Europe hoped to have three stations in the former Soviet republics by the end of 1998.
He said the company saw growing demand for freight forwarding service, which account for a quarter of overall business, in import-hungry Gulf states as higher oil prices boosted business confidence.
It would also invest in warehousing for high-value freight in free-trade zones at Dubai and Amman airports, he said.
Ghandour said the offering of one million Aramex shares at $7 each had been oversubscribed.
"We got good coverage from the Middle East -- mostly individual investors, but there was a big institutional turnout in the U.S.," he said.
He said Aramex might consider listing on an Arab market in future, but for the time being sleepy Middle East bourses could not compete with the high profile offered in the United States.
"The U.S. market is the biggest and the most active and it gives you the capability to tap into a huge market," Ghandour said.
